clue.text: Chris drunk after drop of kümmel and brandy

indicators.note: someone drunk is jumbled and unsteady, so the name's letters stagger into a new order
a drop is a tiny amount, so only the opening letter of the liqueur's name is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of the liqueur's name
the name's letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Chris gets drunk after sampling a little kümmel liqueur and some brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the shuffled name behind the single letter. KIRSCH is a cherry spirit; the surface's own drinks make 'brandy' sit naturally at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Kirsch is a clear fruit brandy distilled from cherries, so it is an example of the spirit named.

clue.text: Similarly situated, like the Owl and the Pussy-Cat?

definitions.text: like the Owl and the Pussy-Cat

blocks.note: first meaning: sharing the same predicament

blocks.clueFragment: like the Owl and the Pussy-Cat
blocks.note: second meaning: Edward Lear's pair went to sea in a pea-green vessel together

explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear's nonsense poem has the Owl and the Pussy-Cat sail off together, so the idiom is also literally true of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means facing the same difficult circumstances as others, and the poem's pair literally share one vessel.

clue.text: Number, small, not odd?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a number that is not odd is even

explanation.surface: A question whether a small figure is something other than odd.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a smart solver to object that the answer is in fact odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven is a numeral, so it is an example of a number.

clue.text: One article supporting hospital's record

the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece backs up a hospital's records.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supporting' puts the single letter and the article beneath the hospital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A history is an account or chronicle of past events, so it serves as a record.

clue.text: Ruth, for example, born at Lincoln?

blocks.note: b. is the standard abbreviation for born
Abraham Lincoln's familiar first name

explanation.surface: A question whether someone called Ruth was born in the city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth looks like a woman's name, but it is the baseball star Babe Ruth; Lincoln is the US president, not the English city.
explanation.definitionFit: Babe Ruth was the famous American baseball player, so Babe is the first name exemplified by Ruth.

clue.text: Title, one held by composer

blocks.note: Lionel Bart, composer of the musical Oliver!
taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer holds a title, perhaps an honour.
explanation.walkthrough: Lionel Bart wrote the musical Oliver!; crosswords often use him as their stock composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A baronet holds a hereditary British title ranking below a baron, so the word names a title holder.

clue.text: Costume worn by a bride bemused army officer

explanation.definitionFit: A brigadier is a senior army officer ranking above colonel, commanding a brigade.

clue.text: Risk daughter's wrath

blocks.note: d is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.definitionFit: Danger and risk are synonyms for the possibility of harm.

clue.text: Fighting with the military in civvies, create diversion

blocks.note: the letters of both words, used as raw material

explanation.surface: Soldiers out of uniform staging a diversion while fighting alongside the army.
explanation.walkthrough: Civvies (civilian clothes) are the opposite of what the answer suggests, which makes the surface neatly misleading.
explanation.definitionFit: Active service is a phrase for duty in an operational military unit, especially in combat.

clue.text: Strangest idea involved a West Sussex town

blocks.note: the letters of both words, used as raw material

explanation.surface: The oddest notion concerned a town in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: East Grinstead is a market town in West Sussex, a county south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: East Grinstead is a town in the English county of West Sussex, so the answer names one.

clue.text: Celebrity's launch, unfinished

blocks.note: a launch is a start

explanation.surface: A celebrity's product launch never got finished.

explanation.definitionFit: A star is a famous performer, a common synonym for a celebrity.

clue.text: Gullible type flourishing? Blow me!

blocks.note: green as in lush and thriving

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims 'Blow me!' at how easily a gullible person is doing well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow me!' reads as an exclamation of surprise, but it describes something you blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A greenhorn is a naive, inexperienced newcomer who is easily fooled.

clue.text: Girl rejected benefit

clue.text: One invested in property in fact

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
realty is real estate, land and buildings

explanation.surface: Someone has in fact put money into property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in fact' reads as a whole phrase, but 'in' is only the link and 'fact' alone is defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Reality is what actually exists, so it is a near-synonym for fact or actuality.

clue.text: Annoyed after golf club medal

blocks.note: an iron is a type of golf club
cross means annoyed

explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the word for annoyed second.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Cross is a German military decoration for bravery, so it names a medal.

clue.text: Set off in time ahead of scaffolder

blocks.note: t is the abbreviation for time
a rigger erects scaffolding and lifting gear

explanation.surface: A scaffolder is set off early, ahead of his workmate.
explanation.definitionFit: To trigger something is to start or activate it, as a verb meaning set off.

clue.text: Tragic romance here in Lombardy

explanation.definitionFit: Cremona is a city in the Lombardy region of northern Italy, so it is a place located there.

clue.text: Mould in shed

second meaning: to throw off or discard, as a snake its skin

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests fungus growing in a garden shed; both nouns turn out to be other senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast is a mould for shaping metal, and to cast is to shed, as a snake casts its skin.

clue.text: A monk accommodating a bishop in a US state

a plus B, the chess abbreviation for bishop

clue.text: Left in making better game

blocks.note: curing is healing, making well again
L is the abbreviation for left

clue.text: Blade wounded girl

a lass is a girl

explanation.definitionFit: A cutlass is a short curved sword, the sort of weapon called a blade.

clue.text: Take rubbish over to cave

taken as written

clue.text: Zeno, say, coming from Cyprus to Icaria

clue.text: A drunken sot is after a pint, ordered as a starter!

taken as written

clue.text: A great deal of land in Kansas I auctioned

clue.text: Take long steps in short trousers

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its final letter

blocks.note: strides is British and Australian slang for trousers
